cards.back: Unequal O–H sharing → partial charges → hydrogen bonding between molecules → every water property follows from this.
Water–water hydrogen bonding → surface tension and continuous columns in xylem.
Water bonding to polar surfaces — capillary action in soil and cell walls.

cards.front: Why is water a good solvent for polar molecules?
cards.back: Its polarity lets it surround charged/polar particles and break ionic bonds — metabolic reactions happen in aqueous solution.

cards.front: High specific heat capacity — consequence for life?
cards.back: Aquatic habitats are thermally stable; body temperature changes slowly — enzymes work in steady conditions.

cards.front: Why does ice float — and why does it matter?
cards.back: Hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open lattice, less dense than liquid water → ice insulates the water below, letting aquatic life survive.

cards.front: Cohesion + adhesion together explain what in plants?
cards.back: Water transport under tension in xylem: cohesion holds the column together, adhesion supports it against gravity.

cards.front: Which water properties appear in Paper 1 questions most often?
cards.back: Cohesion (surface tension), solvent properties, high specific heat, ice density — each linked to a named biological example.
Single sugar unit — glucose, fructose, galactose. Fuel for respiration and the monomer of polysaccharides.
Maltose = glucose + glucose · lactose = glucose + galactose · sucrose = glucose + fructose.

cards.front: Starch vs glycogen vs cellulose — one line each
cards.back: Starch: plant storage (alpha-glucose, helical + branched). Glycogen: animal storage, even more branched. Cellulose: plant cell walls, straight beta-glucose chains, hydrogen-bonded microfibrils.

cards.front: Why does branching matter in storage polysaccharides?
cards.back: More free ends → enzymes can release glucose rapidly. Glycogen is the most branched → fastest mobilization.
Condensation joins monomers and releases water (builds polymers); hydrolysis splits polymers by adding water (digestion).
Glycerol + 3 fatty acids joined by ester bonds — energy storage, insulation, buoyancy (whale blubber).
Saturated: no C=C double bonds, straight, solid at room temperature. Unsaturated: cis double bonds kink the chain → liquid oils, healthier membranes.

cards.front: Lipids vs carbohydrates — energy per gram
cards.back: Lipids store about twice as much energy per gram — richer in carbon–hydrogen bonds, and stored without water.
Glycerol + 2 fatty acids + a polar phosphate group — amphipathic: hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tails → bilayers.
Central carbon with four groups: amine (NH₂), carboxyl (COOH), hydrogen and the variable R group — the R group defines each of the 20 amino acids.

cards.front: Peptide bond — how formed, how broken?
cards.back: Formed by condensation between the amine of one amino acid and the carboxyl of the next (−CO–NH–). Broken by hydrolysis.

cards.front: Protein denaturation — what happens and why?
cards.back: Heat or pH change breaks the weak bonds holding the 3D shape → active site deforms → function lost. Peptide bonds survive — the sequence is unchanged.
Phosphate group + pentose sugar (deoxyribose in DNA, ribose in RNA) + nitrogenous base (A, T/U, C, G).
A–T with two hydrogen bonds; G–C with three. Purines (A, G) pair with pyrimidines (T, C) — constant strand width.
Ribose sugar (vs deoxyribose) · uracil (vs thymine) · usually single-stranded (vs double helix).
